During the field drilling process, each firn core coming out of the drill barrel either naturally broke or was manually cut into multiple segments. For each segment an average density was measured in the field.

Many core segments contain both firn/snow layer(s) as well as ice layer(s) which have distinctly different densities. Yet the measured segment-average densities cannot capture these spatial density variations within segments.
To acquire more precise density profiles, we resampled the densities of all mixed ice-firn and ice-snow segments in 48 shallow firn cores collected in southwest Greenland between 2012 and 2019.

We assigned a density of 862 kg m-3 (estimated ice density for 24 cores by Rennermalm et al., 2021a, and close to the estimate of 873 ± 25 kg m-3 for seven cores by Machguth et al., 2016) to all ice layers.
Then we derived a mean density for the remaining layer(s) of firn or snow, aiming to preserve the original segment-average density.
Resampled firn densities were considered unrealistic if they were less than 70% of the density simulated by the Herron-Langway model (Rennermalm et al., 2021a) or >862 kg m-3.

In these cases the densities were replaced with the average firn/snow density of the nearest firn/snow segments above and below (applied to 0–12.1% of the number of segments per core, 0–5.1% of total length of each core).

The correction of unrealistic values caused the resampled densities to differ from the original segment-averaged measured densities, thus violating mass conservation. However, the differences are small.

For example, for each core (total length varying between 2.915 and 26.68 m), the density of the entire core length after resampling and correction changed by 0–1.9% (average: 0.3%) compared to the original, measured density of the entire core length.
